title: South, east, north, and home again
hook: 1 km south, 1 km east, 1 km north, and you're back. Only at the North Pole?

knows: that walking east follows a circle of latitude
that circles of latitude shrink toward the poles
doesNotKnow: that near the South Pole an east leg can go round a small circle whole times
that the puzzle therefore has infinitely many answers

misconception: Only the North Pole works for the walk 1 km south, 1 km east, 1 km north back to the start.
objective: The learner can explain that near the South Pole any start from which the 1 km east leg goes round its circle a whole number of times also works, giving a ring of answers for each whole number: infinitely many.
keyState: A failing start seen (the walk ends off the start), then two working starts found: 1.159 km (one lap) and 1.080 km (two laps) from the South Pole.

claims.text: From the North Pole, walking 1 km south, 1 km east, then 1 km north brings you back to the start.
claims.source: Every direction from the North Pole is south; the east leg follows a parallel; the north leg returns along a meridian to the pole. Classic puzzle (Martin Gardner; Peter Winkler, Mathematical Puzzles: A Connoisseur's Collection; from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: Starting about 1.159 km from the South Pole, the south leg leaves you on a circle 1 km round, so the east leg goes exactly once round it and the north leg retraces your steps.
claims.source: The parallel at surface distance r from the pole has circumference 2πR sin(r/R) ≈ 2πr. Circumference 1 km at r = R asin(1/(2πR)) = 0.159155 km, so start 1.159155 km out (Demo.tsx startForLaps(1); builder node run, planar 1 + 1/2π agrees to 1e-10 km). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 1 + R asin(1/(2 pi R)) = 1.159155 km.

claims.text: From about 1.080 km the east leg laps twice; from about 1.053 km, three times.
claims.source: startForLaps(k) = 1 + R asin(1/(2πkR)): k = 2 gives 1.079577 km, k = 3 gives 1.053052 km. The simulated walk returns to within a micrometre at each (Demo.tsx walk(), gap by geoDistance on the sphere). The k = 3 figure is quoted only if visited. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 1.079577 and 1.053052 km.

claims.text: Every whole number of laps works, and each gives a whole ring of starting points around the pole: infinitely many.
claims.source: For each k = 1, 2, 3, … the starts at distance startForLaps(k) form a circle around the South Pole; any longitude on it works by symmetry. (The North Pole adds one more point.) | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: These starting points are all on the Antarctic ice.
claims.source: The South Pole lies on the Antarctic ice sheet, about 2.7 km thick there (from memory, e.g. USGS / British Antarctic Survey); every start is within 1.2 km of the pole. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Amundsen-Scott station sits on about 2.8 km of ice; all starts are within 1.2 km of the pole.

claims.text: The plan view is to scale; at this size the Earth's curvature is negligible.
claims.source: Within 1.6 km of the pole, sin(r/R) differs from r/R by under 1e-8 relative; the stage draws a flat plan (105 px per km) while the walk is computed on the sphere. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Relative error of flat vs sphere at r = 1.6 km is about 1e-8.

recall.question: Near the South Pole, why can the 1 km east leg of the walk end where it began?
options: Because compasses fail near the pole
Because the circle you walk east on can be exactly 1 km, ½ km, ⅓ km… round, so you go round it whole times
Because east and west swap at the South Pole
recall.why: If the parallel you reach after the south leg is 1/k km round, 1 km east goes round it exactly k times; the north leg then retraces the south leg. One ring of starts for each k.
